cards.title: Data lives in tables
cards.text: A database is a set of tables, like the sheets of a spreadsheet. Northwind is a small food trading company: its table **products** has one row for each product.

columns.name: product_id
columns.about: a number that tells the products apart. No two products share one.

columns.name: units_in_stock
columns.about: how many units are in the warehouse.

cards.after: Each column has a name. A query asks for data by these names.

cards.title: SELECT picks the columns
cards.text: A query is a request to the database. `select` says which columns you want, `from` says which table.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products;

cards.after: All 77 products are still there. Only the columns you named are left.
cards.tip: `select *` gives every column of the table.

cards.title: WHERE keeps some rows
cards.text: `where` adds a condition. Rows for which it is not true are left out.
cards.tip: Join conditions with `and` (both must be true) or `or` (one is enough).

cards.title: ORDER BY sorts the rows
cards.text: Without `order by` the rows come in no particular order. Add it to sort them; `desc` puts the biggest first.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
where unit_price > 50
order by unit_price desc;

cards.after: The most expensive product comes first.
cards.tip: Without `desc` the order goes from small to big (`asc`).

cards.title: LIMIT keeps the first rows
cards.text: `limit 3` returns only the first three rows. Sort first: without `order by`, "first" means nothing.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
order by unit_price desc
limit 3;

cards.title: OFFSET skips rows
cards.text: `offset 3` skips the first three rows. With `limit` it gives the next page.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
order by unit_price desc
limit 3 offset 3;

cards.tip: PostgreSQL also knows the standard spelling `fetch first 3 rows only`; MySQL has only `limit`.

cards.title: Values repeat
cards.text: Many customers are in the same country, so the column **country** has the same value many times.
cards.after: 91 rows, one per customer, but far fewer countries.

cards.title: DISTINCT removes repeats
cards.text: `select distinct` keeps each different value once.
cards.tip: With several columns, `distinct` drops a row only when all of its columns repeat.

cards.title: NULL: the value is unknown
cards.text: An empty cell is **NULL**: nobody entered a value. It is not 0 and not an empty text.
cards.after: Many customers have no region: the cell says NULL.

cards.title: IS NULL finds them
cards.text: `region = null` finds nothing: nothing equals unknown, not even unknown. Write `is null` or `is not null`.

query.postgres:
select company_name
from customers
where region is null
order by customer_id;

cards.title: COALESCE fills the gaps
cards.text: `coalesce(a, b)` gives `a`, or `b` when `a` is NULL.

query.postgres:
select company_name,
  coalesce(region, 'none') as region
from customers
order by customer_id;

cards.after: No NULLs left: the missing regions say none.

cards.title: LIKE matches a pattern
cards.text: In a `like` pattern, `%` stands for any text (even none) and `_` for exactly one character.

query.postgres:
select product_name
from products
where product_name like 'Ch%'
order by product_id;

cards.title: Anywhere in the text
cards.text: `%` on both sides finds the word anywhere. `ilike` is `like` that ignores upper and lower case.

query.postgres:
select product_name
from products
where product_name ilike '%sauce%'
order by product_id;
query.mysql:
select product_name
from products
where product_name like '%sauce%'
order by product_id;

cards.after: 2 products have "sauce" in the name, although it is written Sauce.
cards.tip: MySQL has no `ilike`, but there `like` usually ignores case already.
cards.mysqlText: `%` on both sides finds the word anywhere. In MySQL `like` usually ignores upper and lower case.
cards.mysqlTip: PostgreSQL's `like` cares about case: there you write `ilike` to ignore it.

cards.title: IN: one of a list
cards.text: `in (…)` is true when the value is one of the list: shorter than many `or`s.

query.postgres:
select company_name, country
from customers
where country in ('UK', 'France')
order by customer_id;

cards.after: 18 customers are in the UK or France.

cards.title: BETWEEN: a range
cards.text: `between 10 and 20` includes both ends: 10 and 20 count too.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
where unit_price between 10 and 20
order by unit_price, product_id;

cards.title: CASE: a label for each row
cards.text: `case` checks its conditions in order and gives the value of the first true one; `else` covers the rest.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price,
  case
    when unit_price > 50 then 'high'
    when unit_price > 20 then 'mid'
    else 'low'
  end as price_level
from products
order by product_id;

cards.after: Every product now has a label.

cards.title: Gluing text together
cards.text: `||` joins texts. Put `', '` between the parts, or they stick together.

query.postgres:
select company_name,
  city || ', ' || country
    as place
from customers
order by customer_id;
query.mysql:
select company_name,
  concat(city, ', ', country)
    as place
from customers
order by customer_id;

cards.tip: In MySQL `||` means OR: use `concat()` there. PostgreSQL has `concat()` too.
cards.mysqlText: `concat()` joins texts. Put `', '` between the parts, or they stick together.
cards.mysqlTip: Careful: in MySQL `||` means OR. PostgreSQL joins texts with `||`.

cards.title: Functions change text
cards.text: `upper()` and `lower()` change the case of the letters, `length()` counts them.

query.postgres:
select product_name,
  lower(product_name) as small,
  length(product_name) as len
from products
order by product_id;
query.mysql:
select product_name,
  lower(product_name) as small,
  char_length(product_name) as len
from products
order by product_id;

cards.tip: In MySQL `length()` counts bytes, so é counts twice: use `char_length()`.
cards.mysqlText: `upper()` and `lower()` change the case of the letters, `char_length()` counts them.
cards.mysqlTip: In MySQL `length()` counts bytes, so é counts twice.

cards.title: Math on columns
cards.text: Columns can be multiplied, added and divided like numbers on a calculator. `as` names the new column.

query.postgres:
select unit_price, units_in_stock,
  unit_price * units_in_stock
    as stock_value
from products
order by product_id;

cards.after: A new column, worked out for every row.

cards.title: ROUND
cards.text: `round(x, 2)` keeps two digits after the point.

query.postgres:
select unit_price,
  round(unit_price * 1.17, 2)
    as with_tax
from products
order by product_id;

cards.title: Whole numbers divide whole
cards.text: In PostgreSQL `7 / 2` is 3: both numbers are whole, so the answer is too. Write `7 / 2.0` to keep the fraction; `%` gives the remainder.
cards.tip: In MySQL `/` always keeps the fraction; `div` divides whole numbers.
cards.mysqlText: In MySQL `7 / 2` is 3.5: `/` keeps the fraction. `div` divides whole numbers; `%` gives the remainder.
cards.mysqlTip: In PostgreSQL `7 / 2` is 3: whole numbers divide whole there.

cards.title: Parts of a date
cards.text: `extract(year from d)` takes one part of a date. Instead of `year`: `month`, `day`, `hour`…

query.postgres:
select order_date,
  extract(year from order_date)
    as order_year
from orders
order by order_id;

cards.after: Now orders can be counted by year or by month.

cards.title: Moving a date
cards.text: `+ interval '7 days'` moves a date a week forward; `-` moves it back.

query.postgres:
select order_date,
  order_date + interval '7 days'
    as week_later
from orders
order by order_id;
query.mysql:
select order_date,
  date_add(order_date,
           interval 7 day)
    as week_later
from orders
order by order_id;

cards.mysqlText: `date_add(d, interval 7 day)` moves a date a week forward; `date_sub` moves it back.
